description: Councils, devolved administrations and the debate over English votes for English laws.
content_html:
Why Government Operates at Different Levels

The UK is governed at several levels: the UK-wide Westminster Parliament, devolved administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and elected local councils across England and the other nations. Each level has different responsibilities, different budgets and different electoral systems. This multi-layered structure means that decisions about a school in Cardiff are made differently from decisions about a hospital in Glasgow or a road in Somerset. Understanding which level of government does what is a key citizenship skill.

Local Government

Local government is delivered by elected councils. Local councils provide a wide range of services: collecting rubbish, maintaining roads and parks, running planning permission processes, providing social care for the elderly and vulnerable, overseeing housing, managing libraries and leisure facilities, and supporting schools. Some of these services are statutory duties (the council must provide them by law); others are discretionary (the council can choose to provide them if it has the funds).

Councils are led by elected councillors, each representing a ward (a local area). Councillors debate local issues, set the council’s budget and hold the council’s executive to account. They are directly accountable to residents: if voters are unhappy with their councillor, they can vote them out at local elections, which in England are typically held every four years. Councils raise some of their own income through council tax paid by local residents; the majority of their funding comes as grants from central government, which means central government retains significant influence over what councils can afford to do.

Key Fact

Local councils provide services including waste collection, social care, planning, roads and parks. They are led by elected councillors who are accountable to residents at local elections. Funding comes from council tax and central government grants.

Devolution

Devolution is the process by which powers are transferred from the Westminster Parliament to elected bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Devolution does not mean independence: Westminster remains sovereign and can in theory reclaim devolved powers, though this would be politically highly controversial. Devolution was introduced following referendums in Scotland and Wales in 1997, and after the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland in 1998.

The Scottish Parliament was established in 1999 and has wide devolved powers, including health, education, justice, housing and some taxation. The Senedd (Welsh Parliament, known as the National Assembly for Wales until 2020) has grown in power through successive devolution Acts, gaining legislative and limited tax-varying powers. The Northern Ireland Assembly operates under a power-sharing arrangement between unionist and nationalist parties, reflecting the region’s political history.

Many students confuse devolution with independence. Devolution transfers specific powers to a regional parliament while Westminster retains overall sovereignty. Defence, foreign affairs, immigration and most taxation remain reserved to Westminster for all devolved nations — the Scottish Parliament cannot declare war or set its own immigration rules. Independence, by contrast, would mean Scotland (for example) leaving the UK entirely, with full sovereignty over all matters. The question of Scottish independence is a separate and contested political debate; devolution is the current constitutional arrangement. Conflating the two will lose marks in an exam answer.

Reserved and Devolved Powers

Reserved powers are those that remain with Westminster. They include: defence and armed forces; foreign affairs and international treaties; immigration and nationality; most social security benefits; broadcasting regulation; and the overall framework of macroeconomic policy. Devolved powers vary between the three nations but typically include health, education, housing, environment, transport (within the nation) and some aspects of justice. The Scottish Parliament has some income tax and stamp duty powers.

Key Fact

Reserved powers (kept at Westminster) include defence, foreign affairs and immigration. Devolved powers (transferred to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) include health, education and housing.

English Votes for English Laws (EVEL)

A long-running constitutional debate concerns the “West Lothian Question”: should Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish MPs at Westminster be able to vote on legislation that only affects England, given that English MPs cannot vote on equivalent matters devolved to the Scottish Parliament or other assemblies? One answer is the principle of English Votes for English Laws (EVEL).

Supporters of EVEL argue that democratic fairness requires English-only legislation to be decided by English representatives, just as Scottish health policy is decided by the Scottish Parliament. Critics argue it creates a two-tier Parliament, complicating decision-making by requiring different MPs to vote on different parts of the same bill, and risks deepening divisions between the nations of the UK. The debate reflects the broader tension in an asymmetric devolution settlement — one in which Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved parliaments but England has none, meaning English governance remains almost entirely at Westminster level.

The extent of devolution — and whether it should be extended, reduced or lead to full independence — is a genuinely contested political question in the UK. Supporters of further devolution argue that decisions made closer to communities better reflect local needs and that democratic engagement is higher when people have genuine power over their own services. They point to Scotland’s different approach to university tuition fees or free personal care as evidence that devolution enables tailored policy.

Critics of further devolution argue that it risks fragmenting the UK, creating inequalities of provision between nations and regions, and making the UK less able to act coherently on shared challenges such as economic policy or defence. Some argue that local and regional variation, while attractive in principle, creates postcode lotteries where citizens’ access to services depends on where they happen to live. This debate has no settled answer and reflects genuine competing values: local democracy versus national unity and coherence.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Discuss question on devolution, avoid simply describing what devolution is — examiners want to see you weigh contrasting viewpoints. Present one view (e.g. devolution strengthens democracy by bringing decisions closer to communities) and then a contrasting one (e.g. devolution creates inconsistency and risks fragmenting the Union). Use a named example — reference the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd, or a specific policy difference between nations. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must add genuine evaluative reasoning: decide which argument you find more convincing, supported by evidence. Watch out for the common error of confusing devolution with independence: state clearly that Westminster retains sovereignty, and that reserved powers (defence, foreign affairs, immigration) remain at Westminster level.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Local councils provide essential services such as waste collection, social care and planning; elected councillors represent wards and are accountable to residents at local elections.
  • Devolution transfers specific powers (health, education, housing) to the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly, while reserved powers (defence, foreign affairs, immigration) remain at Westminster.
  • The “English Votes for English Laws” debate reflects the unresolved tension in the UK’s asymmetric devolution: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved parliaments, but England does not, raising questions about fairness and democratic representation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a reserved power that remains with the Westminster Parliament rather than devolved administrations?
A) Health policy in Scotland
B) Education in Wales
C) Immigration and nationality
D) Housing in Northern Ireland
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) Immigration and nationality.

practice_questions.text: Identify two services provided by local councils in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct services from: waste collection; social care; housing; road maintenance; planning permission; parks and leisure facilities; libraries. Two very similar answers (e.g. “collecting rubbish” and “clearing waste”) score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what devolution means and how it has changed the governance of the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining devolution (transfer of powers from Westminster to regional or national legislatures); 1 mark for a developed description (e.g. following referendums in 1997, the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly were established in 1999 with powers over health, education and housing); 1 mark for a further feature (e.g. Westminster retains reserved powers including defence, foreign affairs and immigration); 1 mark for a further developed point (e.g. the Northern Ireland Assembly operates under a power-sharing arrangement following the Good Friday Agreement 1998). Evaluation not required.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A survey of 1,200 residents across four English cities, conducted by a civic research organisation in 2024, found that 67% of respondents could not name any service provided by their local council, and 78% did not know the name of their local councillor. The organisation suggested this ‘civic visibility gap’ was a barrier to holding local government to account."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about accountability in local government?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the key finding (most residents cannot name local services or their councillor); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (citizens cannot hold councillors accountable if they do not know what their council does or who represents them); 1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. councillors are directly elected to represent wards and should be held accountable at local elections; low civic awareness reduces this accountability mechanism); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests civic education about local government is needed to make accountability meaningful, though the survey of four cities may not represent all areas of England, and awareness levels may be higher in areas with significant recent local controversies).

practice_questions.text:
A cross-party group of MPs is debating whether England should have its own devolved parliament, similar to the Scottish Parliament.

Discuss whether England should have a devolved parliament to address the imbalance created by the current devolution settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear two-sided discussion using named examples on each side (e.g. Scottish Parliament 1999, EVEL debate, West Lothian Question, English regional mayor models). Contrasting viewpoints connected with evaluative language. Substantiated judgement that weighs the arguments.

Secure: Two-sided discussion with at least one named example. Generally accurate. At least one viewpoint developed with reasoning.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly one-sided or without development. Limited or no named example.

Emerging: Basic points about devolution or Parliament. Descriptive rather than analytical. No named example or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
"Devolution has strengthened democracy in the UK by bringing power closer to citizens."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments in support and arguments against, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Devolution has enabled Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make policy choices that reflect their own needs and priorities (e.g. Scotland’s approach to university tuition fees and free personal care). Democratic engagement in devolved elections has in some areas been higher than for Westminster. Bringing decisions closer to communities increases the relevance and responsiveness of government. The Good Friday Agreement, which underpinned the Northern Ireland Assembly, was essential to the peace process.

Arguments against: Devolution has created inconsistency: citizens in different parts of the UK receive different levels of public services depending on where they live, raising questions about fairness. The EVEL debate shows that devolution creates unresolved constitutional tensions at Westminster. England has no devolved parliament, meaning most English governance remains entirely centralised at Westminster. Critics argue devolution has fuelled rather than settled separatist sentiment, particularly in Scotland, where independence remains a major political question.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named real-world examples on both sides (e.g. Scottish Parliament, Northern Ireland Assembly, Good Friday Agreement, EVEL debate). Conclusion that goes beyond “it depends” and makes a substantiated judgement about whether, on balance, devolution has strengthened UK democracy.

Secure: Two-sided argument with at least one named example. Conclusion present but may not fully justify the weighing.

Developing: Relevant points, mainly one-sided or lacking named examples. Conclusion thin.

Emerging: Basic points, largely descriptive. No named example, no substantiated conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: Which agreement underpinned the establishment of the Northern Ireland Assembly in 1998?

Elected representatives who sit on local councils and represent a ward are called _____.

flashcard_questions.a: Transfer of specific powers from Westminster to regional parliaments, while Westminster retains sovereignty.

flashcard_questions.q: In what year were the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly established?

flashcard_questions.a: Defence and foreign affairs (immigration also acceptable).

flashcard_questions.q: Name two devolved powers transferred to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two services provided by local councils.
flashcard_questions.a: Waste collection and social care (roads, housing also acceptable).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the West Lothian Question?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether Scottish/Welsh MPs should vote on England-only matters when English MPs cannot vote on devolved matters.

flashcard_questions.q: How do local councils raise money locally?
flashcard_questions.a: Through council tax paid by local residents.
No — Westminster retains sovereignty and reserved powers such as defence and immigration.

glossary_terms.definition: Elected bodies responsible for providing local services and making decisions for their area, funded partly by central government grants and partly by local council tax.
Elected representatives who sit on a local council, represent a ward and are accountable to local residents for council decisions.
The transfer of powers from a central government to regional or national legislatures, while the central Parliament retains overall sovereignty.
The elected parliament of Scotland, established in 1999 with devolved powers including health, education and justice, using the Additional Member System.
The devolved legislature for Northern Ireland, established under the Good Friday Agreement 1998, with power-sharing between unionist and nationalist parties.
Policy areas retained by the Westminster Parliament and not transferred to devolved administrations, including defence, foreign affairs, immigration and most macroeconomic policy.
Policy areas transferred to devolved legislatures in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, such as health, education and housing.
A constitutional arrangement under which only English MPs may vote on legislation that applies only to England, to address the imbalance created by asymmetric devolution.
